children: Iraq has revived a long-standing bid to approve a landmark federal law that will bring all its oilfields under a single management and allow for revenue sharing.

Parliament has debated the draft federal oil and gas law since 2010 but has failed to reach agreement due to persistent rifts on field management and oil export revenue sharing in the Northern autonomous Kurdistan region.

Iraqi officials reported progress last year in long-standing negotiations between Baghdad and Erbil on the enactment of the new federal oil and gas law but lawmakers failed to pass it after the federal and Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) authorities failed to reach agreement on those issues, leaving it to be debated in the new parliament which was elected in late 2025.
“The former parliament worked seriously to finalise the law, but it failed to reach agreement,” said Zainab Al-Tamimi, a member of parliament’s oil and gas committee.

"The current parliamentary members, especially those from Basra Governorate, emphasise the necessity of finalising the law during this session…I believe there are genuine and serious intentions to proceed with its enactment, as the law has topped the list of key topics discussed recently by the oil and gas committee,” she told the official daily Al-Sabah.
Another MP said the oil and gas law should have been discussed and enacted since 2007 given its importance in defining the rights, obligations and powers within the oil sector.

“The Iraqi oil sector is facing stagnation due to the absence of a federal law regulating its operations, at a time when the old frameworks are no longer capable of keeping pace with the sector's developments,” committee member Banas Al-Douski said.

"The current stage requires genuine political will to enact the law, as Iraq now needs a federal framework to regulate the management of oil wealth, oil sales and exports, and to clearly define the responsibilities and powers of the relevant authorities."

In press comments last year, Biar Taher, a member of the Kurdish Democratic Party, one of the largest parties in Kurdistan, said disputes between the two governments involve mainly revenues from oil exports by Kurdistan.
He said Kurdistan insists that only oilfields discovered before 2005 are subject to joint management while those developed afterwards must be under Kurdish management.
Official Kurdish data shows that Iraq’s Kurdistan Region holds vast natural gas reserves, estimated at 200 trillion cubic metres.
The report by the Kurdish Energy Ministry also said Kurdistan’s proven crude deposits are estimated at 45 billion barrels.

“I believe the oil and gas law is now needed more than ever as Iraq is passing through an important phase of oil sector development and diversification of export routes…I think this law will better organise the oil sector and revenues and also encourage investments by foreign companies,” said Nabil Al-Marsoomi, a well-known Iraqi economist and author.
Another Iraqi analyst said he believes approving the oil and as law represents a significant step in the current circumstances

Sadiq Al-Rikabi, Director of Economic Research at the UK-based Global Centre for Development Studies said Iraq needs to significantly increase its oil production to absorb the shock of declining revenues and compensate for the shortfall in the future.

“Increasing production requires, first and foremost, a stable and clear legislative environment. This can be achieved through the oil and gas law, which provides a legal and institutional framework to regulate the sector's management and contribute to resolving disputes between Baghdad and Erbil,” he said.

“This would enable increased oil wealth, the exploitation and management of oil and gas fields, and the clear definition of each party's responsibilities. Furthermore, it would put an end to conflicts related to certain constitutional issues and financial disputes that have hampered production and the operations of oil companies.”
(Reporting by N Saeed; Editing by Anoop Menon)
